[4/17/2024 3:38 AM] ratyr2 @RayI don't quite understand your question, so I will answer with no. A 25x concentration solution will be this: Read the instructions on the package of MS product and it will say something like, "Use 2.54 g/L". You will then multiply 2.54 by 25 (to get 63.5g) and add the 63.5g to 1 liter of Distilled water. You will then sterilize it. Now you have a 25x solution to take your 20ml from. You take that 20ml to add to a NEW 1L of sterile water. You see, you make the 25x or 100x concentration solutions because often the amounts of a media component you would use is too tiny to accurately measure out. In my example, measuring out 2.54g isn't terrible, but what if it said to add 2.54mg? Getting that right would require a very precise scale, so measuring out larger amounts is easier to be accurate. Once dissolved into that stock solution, using a pipette to draw off 20ml is very easy and can be quite accurate. If you are still unsure, let me know and I will try again to explain another way. {Reactions} 💚 (3) [4/17/2024 3:42 AM] ray000007 Thank you so much. I see what you’re saying now. They have some, but not enough to be considered resistant enough to survive the blight reliably. This is why they want to cross them with the GMO clone. While those crosses of GMO and hybrid may have the same 2 parents, the offspring will have enough genetic diversity to be able to cross with each other. The GMO and the individual hybrids themselves will be able to cross with any wild chestnut, yes, but here is the concern... If the hybrids cross with wild chestnuts, that will dilute the resistance and will not likely survive the blight. The GMO offspring crossed with either the wild type or the hybrid will either have the gene or not (we made sure the final choices to test had only 1 copy of the resistance gene). This is worth noting, but the offspring of the GMO chestnut (the ones that gets the gene pass on) might have higher or lower expression of that single, so resistance levels may vary a little, but it should not be much variance. So what I'm saying is this: if you want to clone up chestnut to help, you should be using at least 2 different offspring of the GMO X 15/16 hybrids and planting one of each near each other so they can cross with each other. Expecting either one to cross with wild type is going to result in a lot of offspring not having much resistance. I know this is getting pretty complicated, so if you are still uncertain, keep asking questions so I can help you understand fully. [4/25/2024 2:14 PM] ratyr2 @Zap233I only used a microwave once to sterilize a batch of media. It worked, but I would not count on it working 100% of the time. It will boil the water, but an autoclave heats things to at least 121C by increasing the pressure (water boils at 100C at normal pressure, but under pressure it stays liquid at 121C). Certain bacteria and fungal spores can survive boiling at 100C, but not at 121C. So in short, you can use the microwave, but expect to see contamination on occasion that comes from your media. If you are willing to accept those losses from that contamination, then you can do it if you wish. Also of note: If you do it this way, watch your cultures closely. When the contamination starts, you may see it before it gets to your plantlet. The contamination will start from some random place in the media. You might be able to transfer the plantlet before the contamination gets to it. [4/25/2024 2:25 PM] ratyr2 @SwevenWondersSterilizing moss would be a tough one. Unless you can find a protocol by searching google (that would be the easiest way to start), it would require a lot of attempts and experiments. If you want suggestions to experimenting yourself, I can give those, but it would likely be costly. Basically you you would first get some moss and "clean it" by getting it to a very small amount and rinse the heck out of it in sterile water, then grow in indoors under a sterile hood. This lets you grow up new material in a "cleaner" environment. Then when you have enough to work with you would "gently" sterilize small amounts of it with different amounts of bleach/time. Lastly, you would make your establishment media with antibiotics and fungicides to kill off any still living contamination. All this may still not work, because the contamination may be an endophyte (meaning it lives WITHIN the host plant). Not all TC contamination is actually harmful to plants in the wild. Endophytes are often symbiotic in the wild, but in TC we disrupt the natural balance and they become a problem. [6/13/2024 3:29 AM] erwin_myco Horizontal is mostly recommended for tissue culture, also all professional tissue culture labs I know here use horizontal. Easy to visualize the sterile work area with horizontal, and know not to reach your hands etc behind it towards the filter. Easier to mess up the HEPA by dropping media or objects against it though. Vertical gives more turbulence at the work area, can cause more person induced contamination, but better if you stack lots of stuff or large equipment inside which would otherwise mostly block horizontal flow and better use of floorspace although modern horizontal ones are very thin now as well. Both have there uses, but both can work fine, personal preference mostly. [6/13/2024 3:57 AM] phototroph Started a thread. Initial Collection and Preparation Collect Healthy Explants: Choose young, healthy, and disease-free leaves or nodes. Avoid handling with bare hands, and use sterilized tools. Surface Rinse: Rinse the explants under running water for about 10–15 minutes to remove any surface dust or loose contaminants. 2. Surface Sterilization Steps Detergent Wash: Soak the explants in a solution with a few drops of mild detergent for 5–10 minutes, then rinse thoroughly with sterile distilled water to remove any soap residue. Disinfectant Dip: Submerge the explants in 70% ethanol for 30 seconds to 1 minute, then rinse with sterile distilled water to reduce phytotoxicity. Bleach Solution (Sodium Hypochlorite): Prepare a 0.5–1.0% bleach solution with a few drops of a surfactant (like Tween-20) to help the bleach adhere to the tissue. Submerge the explants in this solution for 5–10 minutes. Agitation: Gently agitate the container to ensure even contact with the bleach. Rinse: After bleaching, rinse thoroughly with sterile distilled water (3–4 times) to remove any bleach residue that could harm the tissue. [10/29/2024 8:16 AM] mycelium9530 3. Antiseptic Treatment (Optional) For Monstera, which is sensitive to prolonged exposure to harsh chemicals, a mild antiseptic like hydrogen peroxide (0.5–1%) can be used for an additional 5-minute soak, particularly if contamination is recurrent. Rinse again with sterile water. 4. Planting in Culture Media Transfer the explants to sterile culture media in a laminar flow hood. Ensure all tools, containers, and media have been autoclaved or appropriately sterilized beforehand. If possible, divide large explants into smaller sections, as this can reduce the likelihood of contamination. 5. Post-Culture Monitoring and Contamination Control Observation: Monitor for contamination over the first few weeks. If bacteria or fungi appear, remove and dispose of the contaminated explant immediately to prevent it from spreading. Antibiotics/Fungicides: If contamination recurs, consider adding a mild antibiotic (e.g., cefotaxime) or fungicide (e.g., carbendazim) to the culture media, but only for the initial few culture cycles, as they may harm plant cells over time. 6. Environmental Controls Ensure a strictly aseptic environment in your workspace with consistent use of a laminar flow hood. Keep the culture jars closed tightly and avoid handling them unless necessary to reduce the chance of airborne contaminants entering. {Reactions} 💜 (2) [10/29/2024 8:19 AM] mycelium9530 1. Test Tubes Used For: Test tubes are commonly used in the early stages of tissue culture, particularly for establishment and multiplication stages. Advantages: Their narrow design provides a stable, controlled environment for small explants (plant tissue samples). Test tubes are ideal for culturing small, individual specimens that require containment in a sterile and compact space, making them easier to monitor and less prone to contamination. Application: They are especially useful for cultures needing precise handling and protection, such as fragile seedlings, callus cultures, or individual shoots. 2. Polypropylene (PP) Cups with Lids Used For: PP cups with lids are often used in later stages of tissue culture, such as rooting and acclimatization. They can also be used for larger explants or in micropropagation setups where more space is beneficial. Advantages: PP cups are generally larger, providing more room for roots to develop and allowing greater airflow (if the lids have ventilation holes or filters). They are lightweight, durable, and can be reused multiple times after sterilization. Application: Ideal for plants in the rooting phase, PP cups are suitable for cultures that need more substrate or growth medium. They are commonly used for species that benefit from increased humidity control and space, allowing them to better prepare for transfer to soil. Summary of Uses Test Tubes: Best for initial culture stages, individual explants, and environments with limited space and contamination control. PP Cups with Lids: Better suited for later stages, larger plants, rooting phases, and transitional acclimatization. {Reactions} 🔥 [10/29/2024 9:42 AM] mrcon_man Can someone help me [10/29/2024 9:42 AM] mrcon_man I need help so when she says mg what would one mg be for ul? [11/15/2024 6:50 PM] whoknows_77530 just my thoughts Lighting is extremely important for plants at every stage of their development, including tissue culture, as it directly influences photosynthesis, growth, and overall health. Even in tissue culture, plants rely on photosynthesis to produce the energy needed for growth. Photosynthesis uses light as the key ingredient to convert carbon dioxide and water into sugars and oxygen. These sugars act as the energy source for the formation of new tissues, including shoots and roots. Without adequate light, the energy supply is limited, and growth is stunted. Intensity: Tissue cultures are sensitive to light intensity. Too much light can lead to stress and bleaching, while too little light may fail to trigger sufficient photosynthesis. Photoperiod (Duration): The duration of light exposure also matters. Continuous light can sometimes inhibit natural growth cycles, while well-timed periods of light and darkness mimic natural conditions and enhance growth. {Reactions} 💚 [11/15/2024 6:52 PM] 999energie Ah yes no i agree with everything you said I was more concerned regarding needing a specific LED for TC! [12/10/2024 10:37 AM] ebo1744 Do you own the 120-year-old house? If so, you can probably install a wall overlaymentand seal it in. and add a high volume MERV air filter. Turns out that if you exchange the air in a room multiple times through a MERV-13 filter box, you get cleaner air than if you do a single pass through a HEPA filter. This will not work for air input to your TC box, but it will generally clean the air in the room you are working. I will have to dig quite a bit to look for the place I learned about that, but it might help you in your place. [12/10/2024 10:40 AM] ebo1744 You might also look up the procedures for "mold remediation". There are a number of lengthy procedures. You can also look at using an ozone generator - but be careful and follow the directions, as ozone is toxic to living things, so use it and then blow out the air in the room/house. [12/10/2024 10:45 AM] ebo1744 As mentioned to Laur, there was a study that looked at how much gets through each filter type, and how much air goes through. Then compared the same units running for something like a couple of hours and found that circulating the same air in a room through a MERV filter box, got as good or better air than running through a HEPA filter. It will take me some time to see if I can find that experiment, but those are the details I remember. [12/11/2024 6:49 PM] whoknows_77530 heres just what AI says: Callus Induction in Water Lilies: Use an appropriate explant, such as leaves, petioles, or rhizomes. Prepare a sterile growth medium with a high concentration of auxins like 2,4-D (2,4-dichlorophenoxyacetic acid) or NAA (naphthaleneacetic acid) to stimulate callus formation. Cytokinins may also be used in specific ratios, depending on the water lily species. Light Conditions for Callus Induction: Dark conditions: Typically, callus formation is encouraged under dark conditions or very low light. Darkness minimizes photosynthetic activity, which can redirect energy toward undifferentiated cell division and growth of the callus. If using light, maintain it at a very low intensity (~500–1,000 lux) to avoid stressing the tissues and potentially inducing differentiation prematurely. Environmental Parameters: Temperature: Maintain a controlled temperature of around 25°C (77°F). Humidity: Ensure high humidity levels to prevent desiccation. Sterility: Work in a sterile environment to avoid contamination. Post-Callus Formation: Once the callus is established, you can expose it to light conditions to encourage organogenesis or somatic embryogenesis, depending on your tissue culture goals. At this stage, moderate light levels (~2,000–5,000 lux) are generally beneficial. This way you can leave the lid just laying on top of them, while there is no way they can contaminate while trying to get them into your SAB. For example I prepour slants in 50ml centrifuge tubes, I can fit 5 of them in a 1liter glass jar with a lid with airfilter and a little splash of water in it. I sterilize those (let them cool at an angle if needed), and I just open a jar in front of my hood (or sab) once I need a slant. Gives me some stock of sterile slants. The same can be with PP containers, just need to find something where they fit in. Could be anything from glass jars, to cookie tins inside a filtered mushroom bag or something. Once you have shaped it, you can then heat it again, and while at a heat just above "cherry red" quench it in brine, water, oil or air depending on the steel type. So like @Erwin_Myco says, that will work for tools, but he would not recommend it. To think of it another way, 400F is the "light yellow" color that knives and razors are tempered to when heat-treating steel. This would be more than hot enough to sterilize steel tools, but could mess with steel properties over time, and would boil any media until it boils off. [1/31/2025 6:10 PM] thegreatestbenjamin Plant tissue culture relies on specific plant parts that have the ability to regenerate and grow into whole plants under controlled conditions. The key plant parts that make tissue culture possible include: 1. Explants (Tissue Source) These are the plant tissues or organs used to initiate a culture. Common explants include: • Meristems – Actively dividing cells found in shoot tips and root tips, ideal for micropropagation. • Leaf Discs – Small sections of leaves used for regeneration in many species. • Stem Segments (Nodal Explants) – Contain axillary buds that can be induced to grow. • Roots – Sometimes used for root cultures or callus formation. • Seeds & Embryos – Useful for embryo rescue and genetic studies. • Anthers/Pollen (Microspores) – Used in haploid culture for breeding research. 2. Meristematic Tissue • These are groups of undifferentiated cells capable of continuous division. • Found in shoot tips, root tips, and lateral buds. • Used for virus-free plant propagation. 3. Callus (Undifferentiated Mass of Cells) • Forms from wounded or cultured plant tissue. • Can be induced to differentiate into shoots or roots. 4. Somatic Cells (Totipotent Cells) • Most plant cells have totipotency, meaning they can regenerate into a whole plant under the right conditions. • Parenchyma cells in leaves and stems are often used for this. 5. Vascular Tissue (Phloem & Xylem Cells) • While not commonly cultured alone, vascular tissues help transport nutrients in cultured plants. These plant parts, combined with the right hormones (auxins and cytokinins) and nutrients, enable successful plant tissue culture. Are you looking for information on a specific plant species or type of culture? Does anyone know how trademarked named plants work? I know that if a plant/seed is patented, then growing, or cross breeding, and resale of those is a legal issue. With trademarked named things it's just the name that I would need permission to use when labeling a product. What would I do if I didn't get the permission to use the name, outside of using its scientific name and describing it? [2/23/2025 7:03 PM] apteronotus5947 (pinned) If you are in the US then for a trademarked name without permission you would need to use a new name to sell it commercially. If you were selling a line of crossed plants you can use the trademark to “describe” how the progeny was made, like saying your new apple cultivar called “mega crunch” is a cross between honeycrisp and crabapples it allowed but some trademark owners don’t always understand this, the legal doctrine is called nominative use, i.e. the right to say the names of things. You just can’t sell it as that name without permission, and permission be unusual without something like a distribution agreement or extremely laid back trademark owners. This is all broadly true for many countries, but can vary, particularly if the country is not part of the Madrid protocol (which most are but Argentina is a counter example). Keep in mind to think of trademarks as just brands linking a commercial product with its business source or origin, they exist so consumers know what came from who - like an old timey blacksmith’s mark on armor. Because trademarks are designed to protect consumers, trying to get around them with similar names or tricks doesn’t work either, the legal standard is whether the brand would “likely” confuse consumers, not whether a name is exactly copied. Depending where you are located and how big a business you may be starting there are often law school clinics that provide pro bono intellectual property advice to businesses too small to afford a lawyer. {Reactions} ❤️ (6) 👍 [2/23/2025 8:38 PM] deudyscout Can someone pin this ^ {Reactions} 💯 [2/23/2025 10:09 PM] compu_bijou Thank you for your input, very much appreciated! [3/27/2025 6:54 PM] rpd5203 another example with some maths Materials: - 0.5 gram of PGR - Ethanol (as needed to dissolve the PGR) - 100 milliliters of water Steps: - Weigh 0.5g of the plant growth regulator. - Dissolve in Ethanol: Add enough ethanol to a container to dissolve the 0.5g of PGR. Start with a small amount, such as 5ml to 10ml, and increase if necessary until the PGR is completely dissolved. - Add Water: Slowly add water to the ethanol-PGR mixture until the total volume reaches 100ml. Stir thoroughly to ensure complete mixing. - Label the solution as '0.005g/ml PGR' for future reference. Using the Stock Solution: To prepare 500ml of media with a concentration of 0.2 g/liter: Calculate the Required Stock: - Desired concentration in media = 0.2 g/l - Total media volume = 500ml - Total amount of PGR needed = 0.1g - 0.2 g/l × 0.5 liter = 0.1g Measure the Stock Solution: - Concentration of stock solution = 0.005 g/ml - Amount of stock solution needed = 20ml - 0.1g × (1ml / 0.005 g/ml) = 20ml Mix into Media: - Add the 20 ml of stock solution to the media. - Top up with additional water to reach a total volume of 500 ml. note: - This is a lot of PGR for a stock solution, you will probably use less which mean less ethanol to disolve it in. - I kind of picked numbers at random as well. - You can work out the math so that you make the stock solution 10x or 100x the concentration of working solution, to get nice round volumes from the stock for use in media. this particular example is 25x (unintentially) - I would just make an excel sheet with each of the PGRs you might use that does the math for you. {Reactions} 👏 (3) [3/27/2025 7:02 PM] sarahwithanhattheend Yus! {Reactions} ❤️ [3/27/2025 7:03 PM] sarahwithanhattheend Ok awesome. Excited to see how it turns out! [4/3/2025 10:48 PM] rpd5203 bio safety cabinets blow sterile air from the top down on to your samples, so you don't want to pass anything over your samples unless its sterile. its also an enclosed space for the most part, any fungi or what ever will just be filtered out (it filters both the air before it goes to your sample but also filters when it exhausts air). required for pathogens and other deadly things by law. laminar flow hoods blow sterile air from infront of you and at you (horizontally), in this case you want to work in lanes with an open space between between the filtered air and your currently open work sample, and in the back half of the hood (the farther away from the source of sterile air, the more likely it will be less sterile). this also means its blowing what ever from the samples into your face (can not work with pathogens or sporulating fungi like this). i have worked in both and for most of what i was doing it doesn't matter, but i always used a bio safety cabinet when dealing with fungi we were growing (on purpose of course) [4/3/2025 11:36 PM] plantsinjars Why are you getting a bsc instead of laminar flow hood? DNA is extracted and screened for the mutations it has in specific genes of interest to ignore unmutated plants and track how many/what changes were made. selection is made for the mutants that result in beneficial physiological traits and used in cross breeding. the identified mutated genes could be used for marker assisted selection at this point. mutations like this are often lethal, so growing them in tissue culture can keep more of them alive for use in breeding programs. breeders don't care about the sick plants, they want the unique/different genes that might be useful to add into other varieties. It is technically not GMO and a large amount of the food you consume today was made at some point like this. wheat, rice, tomato, barley, corn, soybean, pea, potato, lettuce... What is labeled as GMO are targeted changes, something a lot more specific than random mutation from chemicals that happen anywhere and everywhere in the genome. even if its just moving one tomato variety gene into another tomato variety. genes can be linked and in some cases a good and bad are very hard to separate with regular breeding, so engineering a targeted solution is the only way in some cases. Gently mix it on a mag stirrer until it is hydrated. Then autoclave/ pressure cook to sterilise. Then swirl the bottle until it is visibly homogeneous, but not so much you make it foamy. Put the bottle in the SAB/hood and allow it to cool a little. Agar doesnt set until it gets below 45 C Then pour under the hood or SAB into pre-sterilised containers. The best containers for making media in are called Durran bottles. They have a PP cap which will withstand hundreds of autoclave cycles and they seal really well. You can often find new and used ones on Ebay. Just remember to slightly loosen the caps before autoclaving. Labs all over the world use these bottles for agar media. If you use a flask, cover with foil before autoclaving. Venus flytraps can take up to like 6 years to grow to maturity from seed whereas in culture you can get pretty big plantlets in under a year. The explants tend to start off tiny but grow roughly as large as you allow them to. As for the benefits i'll use my exact use case. I have a carnivorous bromeliad that I want to propagate, and the only ways to do so are from seed (very unreliable and you need 2 parent plants to bloom at the same time, if they don't take you missed your only chance) or by pups that only occur after it flowers. you usually only get 1-3 and up to 5 if you're lucky. You need the full 121 C for 15 or more minutes. The other problem with agar media is that if the media boils in the tube it will easily boil over as the bubbles get caught up in the viscous gel. If you really want to wing it then create a makeshift steamer with a pan of water and a lid and a rack for the tubes. If you really don't want to buy a pressure cooker there is the technique of Tyndallization (google for full details) Basically you heat to 100 C for 15-30 mins on three successive days. Day 1 kills vegetative bacteria and when they cool spores will germinate. Day 2 kills the germinated bacteria and stimulates more spores to germinate Day 3 catches anything left. I've done this in the past to sterilise peptone with various heat labile sugars such as maltose. It works pretty well with about a 1% failure rate. It doesnt work if you do the heatings all on the same day. They need the gap in between, and don't refrigerate between the days because you want the spores to germinate. RT is fine. {Reactions} 💯 (2) 🔥 [6/7/2025 12:38 AM] ebo1744 I would put the lids on, but unscrewed about 1/4'th to 1/2 turn. Then when you are done running through the microwave, screw them on tight. [6/17/2025 9:53 PM] _stevea > I don't really understand what the "Mother Block Room" is. How do they maintain a constant genotype of the plant for such a long time (even 41 years) without worrying about mutations I could be wrong, but I suspect they actually refresh the mother plant from the most successful clones occasionally? Also, the plants exist in extremelt stable, low-stress conditions which minimize epigenetic stressors that might lead to mutations, so there's that. TC is essentially the perfect way to make long-term storage possible without actually freezing seeds or something. Apical meristems are the best source for cloning. Those cells have gone through the fewest division cycles, and have accumulated less somatic mutations as a result. They'll be the truest to the source possible, generally speaking. They're also less likely to be containing viral loads. If you aren't cloning for the truest copy possible, you don't have to use apical meristems. Then the plants will have very slow access to the nutrients and PGR's and will therefore develop more slowly. The ideal is to have a gel solid enough to support the plant and to not slop around, but not too solid to inhibit diffusion. I’ve got a question that might be startling obvious: are explants the same genetic age as their donor material? For instance, if a pine tree was somehow propagated in something like WPM successfully, and the donor was 10 years old, would all clones be 10+ years old if successfully grown and acclimatized to soil? [7/14/2025 2:28 AM] palustral Great question! Age is a funny thing with plants. Yes, the clones would all be the same technical age as the donor plant, but they would not have the same functional age. There is a lot of chemical balances and signals in a plant as it "ages." For example, the number of root tips producing a given plant growth regulator (PGR) signals the other meristems and this balance between root tip PGR's and apical meristem PGR's can signal a plant when to flower, etc., etc. So functionally when we are putting a plant into tissue culture, we are essentially using various PGR's to set back the funtional clock to make the plant multiply or some other growth we want to force the plant to exhibit. Later, we acclimate the plants to start functioning as they would, regulating their own growth. I hope that makes sense. {Reactions} ❤️ (3) [7/14/2025 2:31 AM] sallygbaybee Very much so! In other words, it would turn back the functional clock while the plants were in culture, and then they would “catch-up” once removed from the media? {Reactions} 👍 [7/14/2025 2:32 AM] palustral "Catch-Up" or as I would put it, "start over". {Reactions} ❗ [7/14/2025 2:35 AM] sallygbaybee Ah, so the genetic clones would be considered juvenile instead of established. That clears things up, thank you! [8/13/2025 5:11 PM] davuk_70151 MS medium has no organic nitrogen compounds, because its designed for growth of autotrophic organisms, i.e. plants. Heterotrophic bacteria, the sort which would be on your finger will struggle to grow on MS. However, the cut end of an explant will have a leakage of organic nitrogen compounds. This is why when people get contamination it is nearly always around the explant. All moulds are also heterotrophic and have an absolute requirement for organic nitrogen. There are autotrophic bacteria which will grow on MS, but they will not often be found on your finger. {Reactions} 😮 [8/13/2025 5:13 PM] ._tash._._47104 Oh i see! So a better way to test for contamination would be to cut a bit of explant and pop it into the media without sterilising it? [8/13/2025 5:14 PM] davuk_70151 Well that would add contamination. [8/17/2025 10:45 PM] russ_42145 Thanks, here was my routine:- Clean Laminar Hood with 70% alcohol x3 and leave running Jars and containers added to autoclave bags All jars and containers in autoclave 20mins @126* Once done straight into flow hood All scissors, scalpels trays etc autoclave 20mins @126* then into hood Media made up and autoclaved 20mins @ 126* then into hood IBA Bottle sterilised with 70% isoprope and into hood Media completed by adding IBA Bags transferred into flow hood from vitapod each back sprayed and wiped 70% alcohol Media into each pot\jar and lids on (not sealed) Each plant decanted one at a time, cleaned in distilled water in one bath then into a second I go from left to right and never touch the plant or let other plants touch each other Using sterlized tools, transfered each plant into media, each time running tweezers/scalpel through the ceramic sterlizer Once sealed, spray each container and wipe outside of container/jar with isopropanl Transfer to grow tent [8/17/2025 10:54 PM] doxatek What about explant sterilization [8/17/2025 10:57 PM] doxatek You can make some media containers and let them sit without explants as well to verify your contam is not from your media. Autoclaves generally use heat and steam to sterilise so everything really should be open . Autoclaves work on increasing the internal pressure to prevent boiling above 100 degrees C, this means that any closed vessel is under pressure. The PP cups if closed would collapse - so having lids slightly ajar lets the internal pressure equilise with the autoclave. As far as autoclaving pipettes- we do them in their racks since the boxes don't actuallyy form a seal- we then put them in an oven to dry as the steam still gets inside. In saying that, i have wrapped twisors and sciccors directly in aluminium foil- steam doesn seam to get in, but heat is probably doing the job {Reactions} 💯 (3) 👍 [8/20/2025 2:56 AM] juzzy__ There's 2 things at play here, 1 when it's hot, nothing needs to be sealed tight unless it was designed for that. I've seen people wait until it's cooled off to then carefully reach in and seal them all off (I don't like that one personally) Another option is to move them (sealed?) to your flow hood left ajar and allowed to cool while vented Last way I have seen someone do it is take a plastic trashbag, bleach the inside, remove the hot PP cups with ajar lids and place them inside the bag on the counter and sealed up and allowed to cool like that. I'll try and write a basic method and hopefully you can adjust the figures depending on what you need. To make the caustic soda solution add 40grams of it to 1 litre of water (or 20 grams to 500ml, or 10 grams to 250ml etc). You only need a tiny bit but caustic soda is pretty cheap anyway. Next measure out 10mg of BAP into something that can hold more than 10ml. Use a little bit of the caustic soda solution to dissolve the BAP (only a couple drops), just enough to dissolve it and no more. Once dissolved, top it up with water to 10ml, and now you have a solution of BAP that's 1mg/ml. Divide or multiply those numbers by whatever quantity you need, bearing in mind 10ml of BAP can be enough for 10 litres of media. If your protocol asks for 1.0mg/L of BAP, add 1ml of the BAP solution to 1 Litre of water. If it asks for 2, add 2ml etc Hope that make sense [9/6/2025 12:45 AM] 111r1114314 and can someone else check that, it's very late here and I should be in bed 😇 [9/6/2025 12:49 AM] orangmawas Thank you soooo much!!! [9/10/2025 7:36 PM] juzzy__ I do not, I wrap it with the intent that I don't accidently open a container by lifting the lid, etc. On big sealed vessels I don't bother wrapping them. I have 0 expertise of how contamination works but I feel if surface contamination somehow becomes airborn again and makes its way into your container than it wasnt wrapped correctly. If you think about a deli cup, you squeeze the sides/lid to lift it and hold it. As it flexes it will try to push air out and then when you release the sides it will draw air back in to replace it (assuming you asserted pressure to deflect the sides) The wrap in that example would prevent the air from escaping the vessel to begin with. What are you wrapping? [9/10/2025 7:38 PM] juzzy__ Another thing I always so if it's unvented container like a small deli cup/etc is I will squeeze the sides of the container a tiny bit and look for the deflection on the lid and hold it for a sec to see if the bulge goes down. [9/21/2025 8:23 PM] t0masmort0n Another way to check is to lay out agar dishes open in a grid pattern and then seal them up and check for contam [9/21/2025 8:23 PM] t0masmort0n Doesnt confirm perfectly laminar but it does confirm if it is keeping your area clear [9/21/2025 8:49 PM] ascpete_25859 Anything in the air flow will cause turbulence downstream. Incense sticks (very inexpensive) can be used as simple and extremely accurate test of air flow, performance and turbulence. But your hand and the rest of the 'stick' has to be down stream or out of the air stream, as far away from the smoking end as possible. First test the hood opening to ensure that no air gets sucked back into the opening (eddy currents) by always keeping your hand and the stick above or below (perpendicular to flow) or downstream (parallel to flow) of the filter face or sash opening. Second test to establish flow patterns of every area within the hood or air stream (laminar flow) by always keeping the smoking end upstream of hand and 'stick', eddy currents and flow patterns will be visible. The smoke does not have to be in a straight line it just has to form a 'Steady Plume' that stays together and slowly expand as it moves down stream. You can also easily see how far away from the filter face or sash opening the clean filtered air travels before it becomes turbulent. There will always be some visible turbulence at the smoking end but it should always be visibly minimal and consistent. BTW, your pictured 'Horizontal' flow hood appears to have the 'Vertical' hood geometry per attached photo. {Attachments} https://cdn.discordapp.com/attachments/1223705218944860291/1419395141528981534/1Hood_Alibaba.jpg?ex=6af2be7c&is=6af16cfc&hm=981ede8a9de5037f1e55bf8e5176bd11206d7dc58b924aafa8319e54ec2c5a8f& [9/21/2025 9:19 PM] Deleted User thank you [9/21/2025 9:31 PM] .mia.5928 Do you know who sells subculture ready TC’s? [10/20/2025 5:41 PM] juzzy__ The big thing with SAB is I spray everything down with alcohol, sides, roof, floor, all items going in, (water containers, tools, bead sterilizer, etc, etc) The wait like 20-30 minutes. THEN - Outside of my SAB I start my sealed bleach jars with explants + magnetic stirrer, for 20 minutes or whatever the protocol is. I'll respray everyting inside the SAB again while waiting 20 minutes for the explants to sterilize. THEN spray the outside of the jar down, stick it in, spray everything down again and start working. {Reactions} ❤️ (2) [10/20/2025 5:46 PM] juzzy__ You really want the heavy objects inside the SAB to settle and stick to surfaces with alcohol so as you transfer between your bleach container and the rinse containers, you're VERY calm with your movements, remove the lid (which could have spores on it and on the rim/edge. Once your fingers touch the lid - they are possibly contaminated. So ONLY touch your plant with you tweezers that are straight out of the bead sterilizer. You also never want to cross over your open containers where things could fall or be pushed into your container [10/20/2025 5:47 PM] juzzy__ Dont think "oh I just sprayed my gloves down I can play with this explant some." - lol seems logical but just don't 😄 [10/20/2025 5:48 PM] juzzy__ it also takes time with alcohol exposure to kill things. several minutes. so a quick spray down and getting to it isnt going to kill it all. but it will bind and hold it down while you work [10/20/2025 5:50 PM] juzzy__ Hope that helps, goodluck. MS salts: 2.215 g (half of 4.43 g/L; or half of whatever your label says per liter) Sucrose: 15.0 g Gellan gum (Plant Cell Technology): 1.50 g (3.0 g/L) BAP (1 mg/mL stock): 1.47 mL (pre-PC dose to account for ~15% loss) RO/DI water: to 500 mL total pH: adjust to 5.75–5.80 before gelling/PC (use dilute NaOH/KOH or HCl) Steps Dissolve base ~400 mL water in a 1 L flask → add 2.215 g MS, dissolve. Add 15.0 g sucrose, dissolve. Adjust pH to 5.75–5.80. Bring volume to 500 mL. Add gellan & heat Sprinkle 1.50 g gellan while stirring. Heat to near-boil until fully clear. Add BAP (pre-PC, you’re pour-then-PC) Cool to ~60 °C. Add 1.47 mL BAP (1 mg/mL). Swirl to mix. Pour into 5.5-oz containers 55–60 mL per cup (~8–9 cups). Aim for 8–10 mm depth. [11/6/2025 5:05 PM] ascpete_25859 Maybe too much air flow , reduce if possible... The air velocity only needs to be 80 - 100 Ft/Min (0.4 - 0.5 M/Sec) within the work area (up to 12 in. / 300 mm from the filter face). Inexpensive Air Velocity Meters (under $20.00) can be used to check the speeds. Simple smoke tests can help identify any harmful reverse currents or eddies. Smoke Test; Incense sticks (very inexpensive) can be used as simple and extremely accurate test of air flow, performance and turbulence. But your hand and the rest of the 'stick' has to be down stream or out of the air stream, as far away from the smoking end as possible. First test the hood opening to ensure that no air gets sucked back into the opening (eddy currents) by always keeping your hand and the stick above or below (stick perpendicular to flow) or downstream (stick parallel, and downstream to flow) of the filter face or sash opening. Second test to establish flow patterns of every area within the hood or air stream (laminar flow) by always keeping the smoking end upstream of hand and 'stick', eddy currents and flow patterns will be visible. The smoke does not have to be in a straight line it just has to form a 'Steady Plume' that stays together and slowly expand as it moves down stream. You can also easily see how far away from the filter face or sash opening the clean filtered air travels before it becomes turbulent. There will always be some visible turbulence at the smoking end but it should always be visibly minimal and consistent https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hKIlpwV_uI8 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vn3zjbiOUtY {Embed} Terra Universal, Inc. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hKIlpwV_uI8 Horizontal Laminar Flow Hood Smoke Test This smoke study provides a visualization of the unidirectional airflow and positive pressure inside Terra’s horizontal laminar flow hood. [11/25/2025 12:03 AM] sheikhamin_73548 Thanks [11/25/2025 12:50 AM] palustral Look up information on Live Stakes. What you are describing is simple 'Layering'. We do this all the time in restoration projects with high rates of survival with many species. We use straight branches 1/2 inch in diameter up to 2 inches, 2 to 3 feet long and drive them into the ground leaving about 6 inches exposed. They are cut at an angle on the bottom and flat on top and soaked in water for a day before we plant. We do dip them in a root stimulator gel right before we plant. We do not bother scratching them because driving them into the ground takes care of that. {Attachments} https://cdn.discordapp.com/attachments/1223705218944860291/1442663794382864434/20240826_103746.jpg?ex=6af3051b&is=6af1b39b&hm=e67f171c80380844749bcee0bf561c3da499619a5bc3ffbd0731ef2400751f45& https://cdn.discordapp.com/attachments/1223705218944860291/1442663794932187197/20240826_103736.jpg?ex=6af3051c&is=6af1b39c&hm=bec1cd478cc7a66809573ac8522a83040bdcb5dc282d64f8b3b2387f0b81d276& https://cdn.discordapp.com/attachments/1223705218944860291/1442663795502878840/20240821_090539.jpg?ex=6af3051c&is=6af1b39c&hm=354db40eb64f23c390021cde42b9657c15a5205d728fd495c446bdb81b15c48a& https://cdn.discordapp.com/attachments/1223705218944860291/1442663796324827136/20240517_114614.jpg?ex=6af3051c&is=6af1b39c&hm=76ff4471856afe4476e7acc8737e73962676bc3fe96a8642aeaf832de70794f7& https://cdn.discordapp.com/attachments/1223705218944860291/1442663796836401223/20240411_105127.jpg?ex=6af3051c&is=6af1b39c&hm=3b5c4f55907203c10f94d90c68986ca646ed39d19f11d1838557309ba2ad5eea& https://cdn.discordapp.com/attachments/1223705218944860291/1442663797352566928/20240410_131434.jpg?ex=6af3051c&is=6af1b39c&hm=dba279a163db66ad0bf71f53ba0571a1ddf62e076379b132b89bda0cc0a59c49& {Reactions} ❤️ [11/25/2025 12:56 AM] palustral Those are photos from the same project, many months apart. [12/6/2025 10:10 PM] palustral Buy a bale of promix, some 1020 trays, lumber, and some window screen. All three of those need cold moist stratification. Fill the trays, spread the seed, water them, cover with a touch more promix and get them outside for the winter season. I build a frame with 2x4's and window screening stapled to it to keep the critters out. After a few months, you can bring them inside a seedling house or under lights and they will germinate. Those seeds do not need tissue culture. The only reason to TC those would be for unique sports or for cloning patented varieties. Often those clones have royalties associated with them and have patents and often trademarks. PGRs; BAP (6-BA), IBA, NAA, GA-3 are available for less on Etsy, but quality and expiration dates may be suspect. MS Medium is essentially dilute 'Hydroponic Plant Fertilizer' the MS Vitamins are simply specific Vitamin Supplements. IMO, 'Clean Space' (Bathroom, Spare Room, Closet, etc) with a Room Air Purifier (Winix C535 or similar size), a Still Air Box / Hood, and following aseptic procedures is simplest and least expensive Home Lab setup. I’m getting a flow hood next week from marketplace but right now I only have a still air box. [5/6/2026 1:18 AM] mochaboy Part of the problem is that you can't rewind the growth. You have protocorm like bodies (PLBs) which propagate roots, then eventually shoots - each stage of which involves hormones in different concentrations. You're taking what are essentially fully formed plant (lings) then trying forcing them to produce PLBs. I'm not sure what you're trying to replicate but for whatever species it is, you'll want to identify the apical meristem which has the highest concentration of dividing cells and growth hormones to initiate the regeneration process. By the way, I'm speaking from the perspective of orchids, so it may not transfer cleanly to what you're trying to do. so tl;dr - it's more important to identify the best part of the plant to extract material and kick off the regeneration protocols. I cannot help myself buying the little tc bags from time to time. I get them, on a sterile plate with sterile tools, cut off all of the leaves and roots, treat them with bleach or H2O2 or whatever the species typically calls for, then cut them up and put them in small magenta jars in plain maintenance media. I have also thrown a lot of money away this way, too. Chasing trendy clones can be expensive and prices always drop like rocks. I am really an orchid grower, but the houseplant market keeps pushing and pushing. I have used houseplants to get my orchids into greenhouses that would typically not offer them. According to the South Dakota State Agricultural Extension office, you only need 11PSI but will want to increase your processing time by 5 minutes: https://extension.sdstate.edu/altitude-adjustments-home-canning There might also be other useful and safety info there. BTW, the history of these charts have to do with early Botulism poisoning with food preservation in rural USA. With pressure, the boiling point of water goes up. Botulism takes an extended period of time above 244F to 260F, and you can reach that by putting something in a pressure cooker and cooking it long enough. If you follow the canning recommendations, then you will have *food safe* things come out. For TC work, you do not have to worry about poisoning someone from becoming contaminated with botulism spores, and you do not have to worry about cooking things at temperature as buch. [7/11/2026 10:16 PM] hunter3893 Light meters are nice for research but in practice they won’t help too much. Your plants will tell you if the light is too bright or dim. They will get etiolated in low light and grow slowly, in high light they get desiccation, burnt/bleached leaves, and get hyperhydricity easier. I think it is best to err on the cautious side and get as low wattage light as you can but put it close. Like 10-20watt t5 led on a single 18”x48” bakers rack shelf. This will get you around 50-80umol of light. Which is right in the sweet spot for most things. For reference, I get light damage at about 110umol and see slow growth under 30umol. For alocasia you might want to put the light slightly higher or use lower wattage, they like around 40umol. Monstera can handle more light.
